newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria sure of EMU entry but voters wary.
newsitem.headline: Austria sure of EMU entry but voters wary.

text.p: Austria's government and financial leaders are as confident of being fully fit to join Europe's economic and monetary union by the January 1999 launch date as they are of snow falling in the Alps in winter.
Finance ministers, central bank chiefs and industrial bosses are also convinced Austria will be among the first batch of the European Union's 15 member states to join the single currency, the euro.
"I am convinced we can reach that goal," central bank president Klaus Liebscher says, adding that any watering down of the strict criteria for entry or a postponement was out of the question.
"Not to take part in economic and monetary union (EMU) would be a catastrophe for our economy," Finance Minister Viktor Klima says. "We cannot prevent EMU, we have to join it."
SERIOUS DOUBTS LINGER IN SOCIETY

But a large number of Austria's eight million citizens, who voted in droves to back EU membership in a referendum in 1994, have serious doubts. The government has a hard sell ahead of it to persuade voters that their destiny, and their jobs, depend on closer economic integration within the EU.
Waiting in the wings to reap the support of the disaffected is far-right leader Joerg Haider, champion of Austria's growing band of Eurosceptics.

He and his nationalist Freedom Party saw their vote soar in European Parliament elections in October to an all-time high of 28 percent after a hard-hitting campaign against the Maastricht Treaty, which enshrined the process and criteria for EMU.

Haider's 28 percent put his party almost level with the pillars of Austrian post-World War Two politics -- the Social Democrats and conservative People's Party -- making his party the biggest far-right political group inside the EU and, he hopes, a beacon for anti-Maastricht voices in Europe.
"We want to reform Maastricht. We want a Europe of fatherlands, one that gives power to the people," Haider said the day after the October 12 Euro-election.

The message was heard loud and clear by farmers hit hard by lower subsidies and tougher competition since Austria joined the EU on January 1, 1995. And by blue-collar workers who in the past two years have seen scores of factories close, or being taken over by foreign firms bent on "downsizing".
Unemployment is rising, insolvencies are running at record levels and exporters are struggling to make ends meet.
ECONOMISTS SAY EU NOT TO BLAME FOR SOME ECONOMIC MISERIES

But economists say Austria's economic woes cannot be blamed on the EU and joining the Brussels club simply exposed deep-seated problems of poor competitiveness, a stifling bureaucracy and lavish government spending.
"These issues are all home grown. EU membership has just made it much more pressing to find solutions," said Georg Busch, senior economist at research institute Wifo.

Wifo expects Austria's economic growth to slow to 0.7 percent this year, from 1.8 percent in 1995, and unemployment to rise to 7.1 percent from 6.6 percent. However, unemployment remains among the lowest in Europe at a shade over four percent.

Busch argued that the jobless rate would be higher if Austria were outside the EU and said net foreign investment of 16.7 billion schillings ($1.55 billion) in the first half of this year was already triple the sum recorded for all of 1995.
OFFICIAL PREPARATIONS FOR EMU GO SMOOTHLY
Austria looks odds-on to meet most of the Maastricht criteria for EMU with much progress made in achieving stability in exchange rates, inflation and interest rates.

Furthermore, the Austrian National Bank already fulfils Maastricht treaty rules governing the independence of central banks and has in the past demonstrated its autonomy from government by pushing ahead with interest rates cuts.

Decisions over the preparation of the European System of Central Banks have been left in the hands of central bank president Liebscher and bank director Adolf Wala, without any interference from Klima.
All three men are firm backers of joining a single currency at its launch. Austria put the schilling into the EU's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) 10 days after joining the union.
"It is more important to have a core of stability at the start than to delay the introduction of EMU so that all European Union members can take part," Wala said recently.
As in most EU states, ditching the national currency is a sensitive issue in Austria, regarded as little different from tearing up the red-white-red flag.

With memories still alive of a weak currency and raging inflation in the 1930s, the schilling has become a symbol of stability. It has been pegged to the German mark since 1979, forcing Austria's central bank to follow closely the monetary lead of the German Bundesbank.
FISCAL ADJUSTMENT IS PROGRESSING BUT SOME PROBLEMS REMAIN

Austrians are big savers and murmurings of discontent can already be heard over the replacement of the schilling for a euro that many here believe will be diluted by weaker currencies, making their bank balances worth less.
On other criteria, a European Commission forecast in November showed the budget deficit falling to the target three percent of GDP in 1997 from 4.3 percent this year.
Tackling the ballooning budget deficit forced a government collapse in October 1995 and a snap election.

People's Party leader and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel said meeting the Maastricht criteria was central to his party's battle against Social Democrat opposition to deep cuts in welfare payments, subsidies to state industry and a pensions system out of control.

The two parties buried the hatchet and formed the next coalition, as they have for more or less the past 50 years, ditched finance minister Andreas Staribacher for Klima and agreed a two-year austerity budget to set them in line, at least on paper, for EMU.

But warning signals are still flashing over the country's outstanding debt. Instead of heading towards the required 60 percent of gross domestic product, a European Commission report forecast Austrian debt would rise to 72.2 percent in 1997 from a projected 71.7 percent this year.
Klima has estimated that the debt ratio will be corrected in 1997 to show it "sufficiently diminishing" and approaching the Maastricht's benchmark 60 percent of GDP.
EMU HAS BECOME SCAPEGOAT FOR ANY ECONOMIC WOES

Maastricht may be central to the EU's economic survival but try telling that to the hundreds of men and women who are set to lose their jobs at the Semperit tyre factory in southern Austria because German parent company Continental is switching production to the Czech Republic where labour costs much less.

Or try telling it to the 90,000 construction workers out of a job as their industry slumps to its worst crisis in half a century, or those being made redundant by national grid Verbund or high-grade steel maker Boehler Uddeholm.

It is a dilemma for the coalition government. Big economic and social changes in Austria, which were clearly inevitable, happened to coincide with a period of turbulence within the EU as members struggle towards integration.
For the Eurosceptics, the EU is the perfect scapegoat.

The start date for EMU is 1999, the same year as the next general election. Unless the government gets its message across by then, more disenchanted and unemployed voters may switch their allegiance to the anti-Maastricht party.
Haider, who confidently predicts he will be chancellor in 1999, is waiting on the sidelines.
